sections.summary: The neutral reading presents one of the seven bowl-angels inviting John to see the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters; the section is a narrative transition introducing the Babylon vision rather than a statement about the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Woman on the Scarlet Beast in the Wilderness
sections.summary: The neutral reading describes John's transport to the wilderness where he sees a woman seated on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns; the section establishes the visual scene of the harlot-beast system rather than addressing the believer's standing.

The neutral reading describes the woman's luxurious attire, her golden cup full of abominations, and the mystery-name on her forehead: Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots; the section identifies Babylon's character and identity rather than addressing the believer's standing.

The neutral reading describes the woman as drunk with the blood of the saints and the witnesses of Jesus; the section establishes Babylon's guilt for persecution rather than directly addressing the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Angel's Interpretation Begins -- The Mystery of the Beast
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the angel's interpretation of the beast's threefold temporal formula ('was, is not, is about to come up') as a parody of the divine self-identification, and identifies those who marvel at the beast as those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.
sections.relevance: The phrase 'whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world' (apo katabolēs kosmou) implies pre-temporal divine registration of God's people. The neutral reading notes that 'God's registration of his people precedes history' and that those whose names ARE written do not marvel at the beast -- 'they see through the beast's pretension because they know the truly eternal One.' This suggests a permanence to divine registration: those in the book from before history are those who remain faithful. However, the neutral reading does not address whether names can be removed from the book (cf. 3:5), leaving the question of irrevocability open.
key_phrases: those who dwell on the earth, whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world
the beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction

sections.summary: The neutral reading interprets the seven heads as seven mountains (Rome) and seven kings, with five fallen, one present, and one yet to come; the section is political-historical interpretation of the beast's identity rather than a statement about the believer's standing.

sections.section_title: The Ten Horns Interpreted -- Kings Who Wage War on the Lamb
sections.summary: The neutral reading interprets the ten horns as ten kings who give their power to the beast, wage war against the Lamb, and are overcome because the Lamb is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are the called, chosen, and faithful.
sections.relevance: The Lamb's companions are described with a three-term sequence: klētoi (called), eklektoi (chosen), and pistoi (faithful). The neutral reading identifies the order as significant: 'called first (God's initiative), chosen second (God's purpose), faithful third (the human response).' The sequence 'moves from divine action to human fidelity' -- the faithful 'responded to the call and fulfilled the purpose of their election by enduring.' The neutral reading notes that election is 'primarily corporate and vocational -- God chooses a people for a purpose.' The culminating term pistoi (faithful) indicates that those who accompany the Lamb are not merely called and chosen but have also proved faithful through the ordeal. This implies that the divine initiative of calling and choosing reaches its completion in human faithfulness, and that the Lamb's company is defined by fidelity as well as election.
key_phrases: the Lamb will overcome them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings
those who are with him are the called and chosen and faithful

sections.section_title: The Waters, the Horns' Betrayal, and the Woman Identified
sections.summary: The neutral reading interprets the waters as peoples and nations, narrates the ten horns' turning against the harlot at God's instigation, and identifies the woman as the great city that reigns over the kings of the earth; the section describes Babylon's destruction mechanism rather than addressing the believer's standing.
